items: A point is an exact place with no size; the shortest path between two points is a line segment; a line segment extended forever both ways is a line.
A point shows a place only — no size
A line segment has two end points and a fixed length
A line has no end points
Two points determine one and only one line
A ray is a portion of a line that starts at one point and goes on endlessly in one direction; it is named with its starting point first.
A ray has one starting point and no other end
Name a ray with its starting point first
Same starting point and same direction = same ray
An angle is formed by two rays with a common starting point; its size is the amount of turn needed about the vertex to move the first ray onto the second.
Two rays + a common starting point = an angle
The vertex is the middle letter of the name

notes.h: Straight, Right, Acute and Obtuse Angles
items: A half turn gives a straight angle; folding it into two equal parts gives right angles (quarter turns); angles smaller than a right angle are acute and bigger ones up to a straight angle are obtuse.

Acute < right angle; obtuse is between right and straight
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle

items: Folding a paper circle again and again in halves gives 180°, 90°, 45°, 22.5° … — the same equal markings a protractor has; each halving line is an angle bisector.
Fold in halves to get equal angles
Each fold gives half the angle before
The line of the fold is the angle bisector

Centre on the vertex
One arm through 0°
Read the scale that starts at 0° on that arm
Reflex = 360° − small angle

Base arm first
Centre on the vertex, 0° on the base arm
Mark the degree, join with a ruler

90° right · 180° straight · 360° full turn

notes.h: Numbers Can Tell Us Things: Taller Neighbours
items: Each child says how many of the children standing next to them are taller: 0, 1 or 2. The numbers tell us about the heights and the order of the line.
a number can describe a situation without naming heights
an end child has one neighbour, so can say only 0 or 1
the tallest child always says 0
A cell is a supercell when its number is larger than the numbers in all its neighbouring cells. In a row, a cell has at most two neighbours.
the largest number is always a supercell
the smallest number is never a supercell
most supercells in n cells: n ÷ 2 rounded up
In a table with more rows, the neighbours of a cell are those to its left, right, top and bottom. A supercell is larger than all of them.
corner cells have 2 neighbours, edge cells 3, inside cells 4
swapping two digits can make a number larger or smaller and change many supercells

notes.h: Patterns of Numbers on the Number Line
items: On a number line the gap between marks tells where a number sits. A number is placed by working out the size of one step and counting steps.
find the step first
the smallest number is at the left, the largest at the right
Numbers can be studied by their digits: how many numbers have n digits, which numbers share a digit sum, and how often a digit occurs.
n-digit numbers: 9 × 10 × … × 10
a digit occurs once in each place it can sit
A palindrome reads the same from left to right and right to left. Reversing a number and adding it again and again leads, for 2-digit numbers, to a palindrome.
the left half decides a palindrome
for a 2-digit start the process always reaches a palindrome
for 3-digit numbers it is unknown — 196 is the famous suspect
Times on a 12-hour clock and dates on a calendar can make number patterns such as palindromes, and calendars come back after some years.
write the time without the colon to test a palindrome
10:01, 11:11 and 12:21 are the palindromic times between 10:00 and 12:59
Make the largest number (A) and the smallest number (B) from the digits of a 4-digit number and find C = A − B. Repeat with C. You always reach 6174, the Kaprekar constant.
always keep four digits, a leading 0 counts
3-digit numbers reach 495
the number of rounds is at most 7

notes.h: An Unsolved Mystery: the Collatz Conjecture
items: If a number is even, take half of it; if it is odd, multiply by 3 and add 1; repeat. Every number tried reaches 1, and nobody has proved that it always does.
powers of 2 reach 1 by halving
an odd number becomes even after 3n + 1
Numbers in a middle column can be added (and in the second puzzle subtracted) as many times as needed to make the side numbers. Looking at the sizes helps you do it in your head.
start with the largest number that fits
check the leftover is made by a smaller number
only 1,000 among the thousands cannot be made

notes.h: Digits and Operations: Always, Sometimes, Never
items: The number of digits of a sum or difference depends on the numbers. To decide, use the smallest and largest numbers with that many digits.
smallest 5-digit number 10,000; largest 99,999
4-digit + 2-digit can never reach 6 digits: 9999 + 99 = 10,098
A pattern of numbers can be added quickly by counting equal groups, using the arrangement, instead of adding one by one.
equal numbers: count × number
patterns can be built to give a chosen sum
An estimate is a close, quick guess made with round numbers when an exact count is not needed.
round to easy numbers
break a big count into a known unit × number of units
In a game where players add numbers to reach a target, work backwards from the target to find the numbers that the winner must say.
work backwards from the target
step size = largest add + 1
numbers, patterns and puzzles can all be explored — that is computational thinking

Wrong: the biggest number must be in the middle. Right: a supercell can be anywhere, even at the end
Wrong: a cell has the same two neighbours as in a row. Right: in a grid it can have up to four
Wrong: every number line goes up by 1. Right: the step depends on the two marked numbers
Wrong: a digit sum belongs to only one number. Right: many numbers share a digit sum (68, 176 and 545 all give 14)
Wrong: reverse-and-add takes the same number of rounds for every number. Right: 12 needs 1 round, 68 needs 3, 89 needs 24

Supercells of the row; does the largest number always b...: Yes, the largest is bigger than all its neighbours so it is always a supercell. The smallest can be one only if the row has one cell.
Can a row of different numbers have no supercell?: No, the largest number is always a supercell.
How many 2-, 3-, 4- and 5-digit numbers are there?: 90, 900, 9000 and 90000.
Digit 7 in 1 to 100 and 1 to 1000: 20 times in 1 to 100; 300 times in 1 to 1000.
3-digit palindromes with digits 1, 2, 3: 111, 121, 131, 212, 222, 232, 313, 323, 333 (9 numbers).

No — two 2s would need the middle two children to each be shorter than the other
Mark the supercells in 15 40 22 8 31 12 19

4 — fill big, small, big, small … e.g. 80 10 70 20 60 30 50 40
In 12 40 / 31 22, which cells are supercells (2 × 2 grid)?
40 and 31 (40 beats 12 and 22; 31 beats 12 and 22)

the 3rd mark after 4000, because each step is (5000 − 4000) ÷ 5 = 200

items: Data is any collection of facts, numbers, measures or observations. To find an answer that nobody has written down, we must go and collect data, for example by asking every child.
data is facts, numbers, measures or observations
collect data to answer a question nobody has already answered
a collected list is raw data and still needs organising
Tally marks count in groups of five and a frequency table writes each category with its count. The counts are called frequencies.
data can be organised in a table using tally marks
frequencies are the counts of occurrences
the table shows how many, not who chose
Writing data in ascending order makes the smallest and largest values and the counts of any value easy to find. A frequency table is another way to arrange the same data.
ordered data: smallest first, largest last
frequency of a value is easy to count in ordered data
the same data can be arranged in different ways, each with advantages and limitations
A pictograph shows data through pictures of objects. A key (scale) tells how many each symbol stands for and a half symbol stands for half of that.
a pictograph shows data with pictures; categories can be rows or columns
the key (scale) says what one symbol means
a half symbol means half the scale
To draw a pictograph, choose a scale so that each number needs whole or half symbols: symbols = number ÷ scale. A big scale saves time and space.
symbols to draw = number ÷ scale
use a half symbol for half the scale
a large amount of data or frequencies that are not exact multiples of the scale make a pictograph harder
A bar graph shows each category as a bar of equal width with equal gaps. The length or height of the bar, read on the scale, gives the frequency, so we can compare, add and find differences.
longest bar: maximum, shortest bar: minimum
the scale tells how much one unit length is
a bar graph is quicker than a pictograph when the data is large

To draw a bar graph, draw two perpendicular lines, write the categories with equal spacing, choose a scale starting from zero and draw each bar with length = value ÷ scale, all of the same width and with equal gaps.
choose the scale from the smallest and largest values so the graph fits
bar length = value ÷ scale
the markings of the unit lengths start from zero

The same data can be drawn with horizontal or vertical bars. Heights measured upwards from the ground are better shown with vertical bars (a column graph); lengths along the ground are better shown with horizontal bars.
heights measured upwards: vertical bars (column graph)
lengths parallel to the ground: horizontal bars
bars of equal width let us compare only the heights

An infographic is a data graph beautified with pictures to communicate faster, but a prettier picture can mislead, for example when taller triangles are also wider or a drawing looks twice as tall as the numbers say.
infographics use attention-attracting visuals
bars of equal width make clear that only heights are compared
be careful when making or reading infographics
Wrong: every question needs us to collect data. Right: a fact such as the capital of India or the date of independence is already known; we collect data only when the answer is not written anywhere
Wrong: the fifth tally mark is just another upright line. Right: the fifth mark is drawn across the four so every group means five
Wrong: arranging data in order changes the data. Right: the values and their counts stay the same; only the order changes, so questions become easier
Wrong: every symbol means 1. Right: read the key first: one symbol can stand for 1, 4, 5 or 10
Wrong: we can always use 1 symbol for 1 unit. Right: with 30 or 215 students that is slow and uses a lot of space; choose a bigger scale
Wrong: count the number of bars to get the value. Right: the value is the length or height of the bar read on the scale

items: All the points at a fixed distance from a point P make a circle. P is the centre and the fixed distance is the radius. A compass keeps that distance fixed while the pencil turns, so it draws the whole circle at once.

notes.h: Line of Symmetry and Mirror Halves
items: A figure has symmetry when its parts repeat in a definite pattern. A line that cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded is a line of symmetry.
symmetry: parts repeat in a definite pattern
line of symmetry: fold along it and the two parts overlap exactly
a figure may have a line of symmetry or none

notes.h: Figures with More Than One Line of Symmetry
items: A figure can have several lines of symmetry: a square has 4 (two diagonals, a vertical and a horizontal), but the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square is not a line of symmetry.
square: 4 lines
rectangle (not a square): 2 lines, its diagonal is not one
equilateral triangle 3 lines, regular hexagon 6 lines
When a figure is reflected along its line of symmetry, each part goes onto the other side; a corner on the line stays where it is. A figure with a line of symmetry has reflection symmetry.
reflection: each part goes to the other side of the line
a point on the line stays; other points swap with their partners
to complete a figure, reflect every point of the half

notes.h: Making Symmetric Shapes: Ink Blots, Cutting and Punching
items: Symmetric shapes can be made by folding: ink on one half, a cut on a folded sheet, or a hole punched in a folded sheet. The fold is the line of symmetry and every mark is repeated on the other side of it.
fold line = line of symmetry
one fold doubles every mark, two folds make four copies
a cut at the corner where two folds meet makes a hole in the centre

notes.h: Rotational Symmetry: Centre and Angle of Symmetry
items: A figure has rotational symmetry when it looks exactly the same after a turn of strictly between 0 and 360 degrees about a fixed point called the centre of rotation. Such a turn is an angle of symmetry; 360 degrees is always one.
centre of rotation: the fixed point of the turn
angle of symmetry: a turn after which the figure looks the same
360 degrees is always an angle of symmetry

notes.h: Radial Arms: Angles of Symmetry from the Gaps
items: A figure with radial arms has rotational symmetry only if the gaps between neighbouring arms are equal; n equal gaps of 360 divided by n degrees give exactly n angles of symmetry.
equal gaps needed
smallest angle = 360 divided by the number of arms
360 divided by 7 = 51 and 3/7 degrees

notes.h: Angles of Symmetry Are Multiples of the Smallest Angle
items: All angles of symmetry of a figure are multiples of its smallest angle, and the last one is 360. So the smallest angle, when a natural number, is a factor of 360, and the number of angles is the order of rotational symmetry.
angles are multiples of the smallest
smallest angle is a factor of 360
order = number of angles
A circle fits onto itself after every turn about its centre, so every angle is an angle of symmetry, and every diameter is a line of symmetry.
every angle is an angle of symmetry
every diameter is a line of symmetry
wheels, fans and flowers have rotational symmetry
Some figures have a line of symmetry but no angle of symmetry, some have angles but no lines, and some have both; regular shapes with n equal sides have n lines and n angles.
regular n-sided shape: n lines, n angles
kite: line only; parallelogram: rotation only
Ashoka Chakra: 24 lines and 24 angles
Wrong: any line through the middle of a figure is a line of symmetry. Right: only a line whose two halves overlap exactly when folded is a line of symmetry
Wrong: every diagonal of every four-sided figure is a line of symmetry. Right: a diagonal is a line of symmetry for the square but not for a rectangle that is not a square
Wrong: every corner moves in a reflection. Right: a corner that lies on the line of symmetry stays where it is
Wrong: an ink blot opened is just a random mess. Right: the blot is symmetric: its fold line is a line of symmetry
Wrong: a figure with no line of symmetry has no symmetry at all. Right: a windmill has no line of symmetry but has rotational symmetry
Wrong: any 3 arms give 3 angles of symmetry. Right: the 3 gaps must all be 120 degrees

notes.h: Positive, Negative and Zero: Floors of the Building of Fun
items: Numbers can lie below 0. Counting from a reference (ground floor = 0), floors above are positive, floors below are negative, and 0 itself is neither. The same number tells the floor and the button presses needed to reach it from 0. Positive and negative numbers with 0 are called integers.
floors above the reference are positive, below are negative, the reference is 0
the floor number and the button presses it needs are the same number
integers go on for ever in both directions

notes.h: Adding Integers: Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor
items: Adding integers means moving: Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor. Several presses combine into one movement. A number and its inverse add to 0, which brings you back to the start.
Start + Movement = Target
combining button presses is addition
a number plus its inverse is 0; inverse of 0 is 0

notes.h: Comparing Integers: Which Floor Is Lower?
items: The lower floor has the smaller number. So every negative number is less than 0 and every positive number is greater than 0, and among negatives the one nearer to 0 is greater: -4 < -3.
negative < 0 < positive
between two negatives, the one nearer 0 is greater
smaller numbers are lower floors

notes.h: Subtracting Integers: Which Button to Press?
items: Subtraction as 'making equal': Starting + ? = Target, so Target - Starting = Movement needed. Subtracting a negative number gives the same answer as adding the corresponding positive number.
Target - Start = Movement needed
subtraction is the missing number to be added
subtracting a negative = adding the positive

notes.h: Integers on the Number Line and the Unmarked Number Line
items: The infinite lift turned sideways is the number line: negative numbers lie to the left of 0, positive to the right, and smaller numbers are to the left of bigger ones. An unmarked number line shows only 0 and lets us add and subtract big integers. Subtraction can always be turned into adding the inverse.
left of 0 negative, right of 0 positive
smaller numbers lie to the left
a - b = a + (inverse of b)

A positive token is +1, a negative token is -1, and one of each is a zero pair worth 0. Add by putting out tokens and removing zero pairs. Subtract by taking tokens away; when there are not enough, put out extra zero pairs first.
+ token and - token make a zero pair
subtract by taking away; add zero pairs when short
tokens give the same answers as the lift and the number line

notes.h: Integers in Real Life: Credits and Debits, Heights, Temperatures
items: Positive and negative numbers show opposite directions from a reference: credits and debits in a bank account, heights above and below sea level, and temperatures above and below the freezing point of water. The total of all credits and debits is the balance and can be negative.
credit +, debit -; balance = total
above sea level +, below -
above freezing +, below freezing -

notes.h: Integer Puzzles: Border Sums, the Amazing Grid and Dice
items: Integer operations can be explored through puzzles. In a hollow grid the four sides can have the same border sum; in the amazing grid every choice of one number from each row and column gives the same total, because each cell is a row number plus a column number.
border sums can be equal on all four sides
the amazing grid total comes from the structure of the grid
choose the order of adding and subtracting to move well in the game

notes.h: A Pinch of History: Brahmagupta's Rules
items: Negative numbers were first used in accounting in China and India. Brahmagupta (628 CE) gave rules for adding and subtracting positive numbers, negative numbers and zero. Every rule can be explained with the lift or the number line.
five rules for addition and five for subtraction
each rule matches a movement on the lift or number line
subtraction of an integer is addition of its inverse
